title: Data-driven surrogate models for forecasting experimentally measured fluid flows
authors: Peter I. Renn, Emily H. Palmer, Cong Wang, Morteza Gharib
abstract: Data-driven modeling shows significant promise for faster-than-real-time forecasting of fluid flows. For real-world engineering applications (e.g., flow control), models must contend with limited, imperfect, and incomplete experimental measurements. In this work, we present an analysis of data-driven surrogate models trained to forecast the time-evolution of experimentally measured cylinder wakes in the subcritical vortex shedding regime. Using a dataset of two-dimensional, two-component particle image velocimetry measurements, we train fully convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, Fourier neural operators, and dynamic mode decomposition-based models to forecast the development of experimentally measured velocity fields. To characterize data-driven approaches contending with transient flow features and limited, imperfect observations, the development of predictions over extended forecast horizons is examined at a fixed Reynolds number (Re = 590). Next, models are trained at a range of Reynolds numbers (Re = 230 to Re = 2920) to investigate the impact of increasingly turbulent and three-dimensional flow phenomena, and the challenges associated with measuring them, on forecast quality. We find that experimentally trained surrogate models can provide meaningful predictions over short time horizons, propagate low-frequency dynamics over longer forecast periods, and achieve faster-than-real-time evaluation. However, the data-driven models struggle to preserve transient flow features and high-frequency energy content when faced with noisy measurements and incomplete state observations. This emphasizes the underlying challenges that remain for data-driven modeling approaches to effectively contend with fluid dynamics in real-world engineering applications, where observations are often imperfect and limited.

infographic.key_insight: Experimentally trained surrogate models can forecast cylinder-wake evolution faster than real time, but their accuracy degrades as flow details become more transient, noisy, and high frequency.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This work shows how learned flow models could support practical flow control and prediction from imperfect PIV measurements, while highlighting the limits engineers must account for in real-world sensing.
method: Train fully convolutional neural networks, U-Nets, Fourier neural operators, and DMD-based models
Use 2D, 2-component PIV cylinder-wake data for time-evolution forecasting
Evaluate both fixed-Re long-horizon prediction and multi-Re generalization from Re = 230 to 2920
infographic.evidence_signal: Models produced meaningful short-horizon forecasts and faster-than-real-time inference, but struggled to preserve transient structures and high-frequency energy under noisy, incomplete observations.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may drop sharply when measurements are incomplete or imperfect, especially for more turbulent and three-dimensional flow regimes.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven surrogate models for forecasting experimentally measured fluid flows

title: Collective Bubble Nucleation: Scale-Separated Hydrodynamic Control of Site Stability and Vapor Removal
authors: Rameez Iqbal, Gautier Rouaze, Gio Bellone, Francesco Minola, Lenan Zhang, Zhengmao Lu
abstract: Interactions between boiling bubbles are well known to influence departure dynamics and heat transfer, yet their role in governing nucleation stability, whether sites activate reproducibly, persist, and deactivate under changing thermal loads, remains poorly understood. Here we show that nucleation can be a collective process: neighboring sites at close spacings exhibit reduced variability and sustained activity, consistent with a non-local hydrodynamic shielding mechanism whereby neighboring bubbles slow the intervening flow, reducing convective heat removal and stabilizing vapor embryos. To isolate near-wall nucleation dynamics from bubble-scale vapor removal, we design surfaces comprising pairs of cavities, with intra-pair spacing tuned to the boundary layer scale and inter-pair separation to the departure diameter scale. While the former governs nucleation behavior, the latter governs collective vapor removal once sites are fully active, yielding transitions between excessive, promotive, and isolated departure regimes. Together these results establish a multiscale framework for designing robust, high-performance boiling surfaces.

infographic.key_insight: Bubble nucleation can be a collective, scale-separated process: nearby sites stabilize each other through hydrodynamic shielding, while larger-spacing interactions control vapor removal and departure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Designing cavity pairs with tuned spacing can make boiling surfaces more reliable and higher-performing by controlling site activation stability and bubble removal regime independently.
method: Built boiling surfaces with cavity pairs.
Varied intra-pair spacing at boundary-layer scale and inter-pair spacing at departure-diameter scale.
Separated near-wall nucleation effects from collective vapor-removal dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports reduced nucleation variability and sustained activity for closely spaced sites, plus distinct excessive, promotive, and isolated departure regimes as spacing changes.
infographic.watch_item: The multiscale design appears geometry- and regime-dependent, so transfer to other fluids, heat fluxes, or surface materials may require re-tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Collective Bubble Nucleation: Scale-Separated Hydrodynamic Control of Site Stability and Vapor Removal

title: Flow behind the Imperial Front Wing: comparison of results from volumetric PTV experiment and Nektar++ simulations
authors: Isabella Fumarola, Alexandra I. Liosi, Parv Khurana, Adam Meziane, Isaac Balbolia, Sherwin J. Spencer
abstract: High-fidelity simulations are increasingly adopted, due to advances in computational power and methods such as Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) and hybrid Large-Eddy Simulation (LES). These approaches are particularly valuable for unsteady flows around complex geometries at high Reynolds numbers; however they still require careful experimental validation. Planar and stereo Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) are widely used for measurements but limited by measurement-plane selection and their ability to capture vortices shapes and trajectories. This motivates the growing interest in volumetric techniques, historically difficult to implement in industrial settings. Recent advances in Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) for measuring flows over large volumes make this approach suitable for validating numerical simulations of complex flows.This study compares volumetric PTV measurements against high-fidelity LES to assess the capabilities and limitations for industrial flows. The aim is to establish a benchmark PTV dataset for motorsport aerodynamics using the Shake-The-Box algorithm. The experiment was carried out in the 10x5 wind tunnel at Imperial College London equipped with a rolling road for ground effect simulation and capable of testing up to 50% scale F1 model. Volumetric PTV measurements were performed downstream of the open-source Imperial Front Wing (IFW) at Re=74896. Results are compared with planar PIV studies and implicit LES simulation using spectral h/p elements in Nektar++. This work addresses open questions in the literature concerning the wake of the IFW. Good quantitative agreement is observed in the wake topology. A previously unreported vortex is identified which has the key role of preventing the merging of other dominant structures. These results demonstrate the suitability of PTV and STB for industrial applications while providing a benchmark dataset for the IFW.

infographic.key_insight: Volumetric PTV with Shake-The-Box and high-fidelity LES agree well on the Imperial Front Wing wake, and the study reveals a previously unseen vortex that helps keep the dominant wake structures from merging.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work provides a benchmark dataset and validation path for using volumetric flow measurements and LES in industrial aerodynamics, especially for complex motorsport wakes.
method: Volumetric Particle Tracking Velocimetry (PTV) using Shake-The-Box in the Imperial College 10x5 wind tunnel
Implicit LES of the Imperial Front Wing wake in Nektar++ with spectral h/p elements
Comparison against earlier planar PIV to assess wake topology and vortex dynamics
infographic.evidence_signal: At Re=74,896, the measured volumetric wake structure showed good quantitative agreement with the Nektar++ LES results, including identification of a previously unreported vortex.
infographic.watch_item: Volumetric PTV is powerful but still sensitive to experimental setup quality, particle tracking performance, and the challenge of validating complex 3D wake structures in industrial environments.
infographic.paper_title: Flow behind the Imperial Front Wing: comparison of results from volumetric PTV experiment and Nektar++ simulations

title: Effects of mean flow skew on turbulent shear layers. Part II. Experimental investigation
authors: Dipendra Gupta, Vedant Kumar, Johan Larsson, Gregory P. Bewley
abstract: Planar turbulent mixing layers, formed by the interactions of two parallel streams with different velocities, have been studied far more than three dimensional (3D) turbulent mixing layers, in which the incoming streams are skewed, and not parallel. Yet many practical shear flows are 3D. Here, we develop and validate an experimental methodology to generate and characterize skewed turbulent mixing layers and to quantify how mean-flow skew modifies mixing layer dynamics. We introduce skew with a spanwise deflection of the mean flow using turning vanes mounted near the trailing edge of a splitter plate, and we use cross-wire anemometry to investigate the downstream evolution of the flow. Relative to the planar configuration, the skewed mixing layer exhibits systematic reductions in both mean and turbulent quantities, with deviations reaching approximately 40\%. Despite these quantitative differences, the fundamental characteristics of the mixing layer remain largely unchanged. Mean-velocity profiles collapse under similarity scaling, shear-layer thicknesses retain approximately linear downstream growth, and Reynolds-stress profiles preserve their characteristic near-Gaussian form. Townsend's structure parameter, which quantifies the efficiency of turbulent momentum transport, remains approximately invariant between the planar and skewed configurations, in contrast to skewed turbulent boundary layers, wherein comparable mean flow skewing reduces the parameter by approximately 30\%. These results indicate that mean flow skew modifies turbulent mixing layers quantitatively while exerting only a secondary influence on their underlying dynamics. This study establishes a controlled experimental framework and empirical benchmark for future investigations of three-dimensional free-shear turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Introducing spanwise mean-flow skew into a turbulent mixing layer changes the magnitudes of mean and turbulent quantities by up to about 40%, but leaves the layer’s core self-similar dynamics largely intact.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For 3D shear flows in aerospace, propulsion, and mixing devices, mean-flow skew should be treated as a quantitative modifier of performance rather than a fundamental change in mixing-layer behavior.
method: Added skew using turning vanes near a splitter-plate trailing edge.
Measured downstream flow evolution with cross-wire anemometry.
Compared planar and skewed configurations using similarity scaling and Reynolds-stress profiles.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports systematic reductions in mean and turbulent quantities of roughly 40% in the skewed case, while key similarity features and Townsend’s structure parameter remained approximately unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: The setup is experimentally controlled, but the findings come from a specific free-shear configuration, so transfer to other 3D turbulent flows may require revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: Effects of mean flow skew on turbulent shear layers. Part II. Experimental investigation

title: Geometry-Aware Anisotropic Boundary Correction for Aerodynamic Simulation
authors: Xin Zhang, Yipeng Huang, Shu Jiang, Zhenzhong Wang, Min Jiang
abstract: Aerodynamic simulation is a key component of engineering shape design, where core quantities such as the surface pressure coefficient strongly depend on flow dynamics near solid boundaries. Neural operators provide an efficient alternative to expensive Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) solvers. However, conventional methods treat the boundary region isotropically, failing to account for the distinct physical behaviors along the boundaries. In reality, the aerodynamic process exhibits anisotropy: along the tangential direction, flow propagates along the wall; along the normal direction, physical quantities are constrained by the wall. To explicitly model the distinct physical behaviors, we propose GeoABC, a geometry-conditioned anisotropic boundary correction framework. GeoABC leverages the boundary geometries to introduce direction-aware boundary correction into the intermediate representations of neural operators, transforming boundary geometry from static input features into a structural prior that modulates physical prediction. On 2D airfoil and 3D car tasks, GeoABC consistently adapts to multiple neural operator backbones, reducing near-boundary relative $L_2$ error by $\sim$38\% on average, narrowing the structural near-wall gap shared by mainstream neural operators, and advancing neural operators toward high-fidelity aerodynamic simulation.

infographic.key_insight: GeoABC makes neural operators boundary-aware by using wall geometry to apply different corrections along tangential and normal directions, better matching near-wall aerodynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves surrogate CFD accuracy where it matters most for design: surface-pressure and other near-boundary quantities that strongly affect aerodynamic performance.
method: Geometry-conditioned boundary correction injected into intermediate neural-operator features
Anisotropic treatment of boundary physics: tangential propagation vs. normal constraint
Pluggable across multiple neural operator backbones
infographic.evidence_signal: On 2D airfoil and 3D car benchmarks, GeoABC reduces near-boundary relative L2 error by about 38% on average and narrows the near-wall performance gap.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on reliable boundary geometry encoding and may require extra care to transfer across meshes, shapes, or CFD settings with different wall-resolution quality.
infographic.paper_title: Geometry-Aware Anisotropic Boundary Correction for Aerodynamic Simulation

title: Optimal heat transport at the edge of energy stability
authors: Zijing Ding, Baole Wen, Hui Li
abstract: Large heat flux is commonly associated with vigorous convection and turbulent mixing. Here, we show that this connection is not fundamental. Using a marginal energy-stability theory, we identify near-optimal convective heat transport with the saturation of an energy-stability constraint rather than with turbulence intensity. The theory selects mean temperature profiles whose fluxes closely approach the best available optimal transport states and rigorous upper bounds, predicting the asymptotic scaling $Nu\sim0.0245Ra^{1/2}$ at large Rayleigh number. These profiles exhibit a hierarchical structure consisting of conductive inner layers, logarithmic-like intermediate layers, and a stably stratified bulk, closely mirroring optimal transport calculations and suggesting that maximal convective heat transport emerges near marginal energy stability. More strikingly, the same profiles can be converted into exact conductive states through prescribed internal thermal forcing. Direct numerical simulations show that an initially turbulent flow then relaxes to a motionless state while maintaining a large wall heat flux. Energy-stability saturation therefore provides both a physical interpretation of transport limits and a route to high-flux heat transfer without turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: Maximal convective heat transport is governed by marginal energy stability, not by turbulence intensity, and can occur with near-optimal mean temperature profiles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests a route to high wall heat flux in thermal systems without sustaining turbulence, potentially enabling more efficient heat-transfer designs.
method: Used marginal energy-stability theory to identify near-optimal mean temperature profiles.
Compared predicted fluxes with optimal transport states and rigorous upper bounds.
Constructed equivalent internally forced conductive states and tested them in DNS.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports asymptotic scaling Nu ~ 0.0245 Ra^{1/2} and DNS showing a turbulent flow relaxes to a motionless high-flux state.
infographic.watch_item: The conductive high-flux state relies on prescribed internal thermal forcing, so practical implementation may be difficult in real devices.
infographic.paper_title: Optimal heat transport at the edge of energy stability

title: Numerical simulations of transition and long-term response of a wind turbine airfoil
authors: Thales Coelho Leite Fava, Niels Sørensen, Dan Henningson, Ardeshir Hanifi
abstract: Numerical simulations are performed for an FFA-W3 wind-turbine airfoil corresponding to a section of the DTU 10-MW Reference Wind Turbine. Wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) are carried out with Nek5000 and EllipSys at chord Reynolds number $Re_c=1\times10^5$ and effective angle of attack $AoA=3.1^\circ-3.3^\circ$. A spanwise domain width of 10 percent of the chord is sufficient to reproduce the time-averaged flow and the evolution of the main disturbances. EllipSys is validated against Nek5000 for LES, showing close agreement for the mean flow and most amplified perturbations. EllipSys underpredicts the amplitude of Tollmien-Schlichting waves in the attached boundary layer, owing to higher numerical dissipation, but closely predicts the evolution of the Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) mode in the laminar separation bubble, in agreement with parabolized stability equation (PSE) results. The mode shape is extracted using spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD), revealing the KH wavepacket forming in the separation bubble. Long-time EllipSys simulations show a slow modulation of the normal-force coefficient, with amplitude 10.5 percent and period 48 flow-through times, corresponding to $f=f^*c/U_\infty=0.021$ and $St=f\sin(AoA)=0.0012$. This frequency is associated with low-frequency oscillations reported in airfoil studies, although the Strouhal number is lower than previously observed and occurs at smaller angle of attack. For the DTU 10-MW turbine, the oscillation period corresponds to 7.7 blade rotations. Periodic stalling and reattachment may trigger the oscillation, while sufficiently high reverse flow on both sides of the airfoil may permit absolute instability and periodic bubble bursting.

infographic.key_insight: Wall-resolved LES shows that the DTU 10-MW airfoil’s separation-bubble dynamics are dominated by a Kelvin-Helmholtz wavepacket, while the long-time lift/normal-force response exhibits a slow low-frequency oscillation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results help predict transition, separation, and unsteady loading on wind-turbine blades, informing airfoil design and aeroelastic/load mitigation.
method: Wall-resolved LES with Nek5000 and EllipSys at Re_c = 1e5 and AoA = 3.1°–3.3°
Cross-code validation against Nek5000, plus PSE and SPOD to identify instability modes
Long-time EllipSys simulations to quantify low-frequency force modulation
infographic.evidence_signal: A 10% chord spanwise domain reproduced the mean flow and dominant disturbances, and EllipSys agreed closely with Nek5000 except for underpredicted Tollmien-Schlichting amplitudes.
infographic.watch_item: EllipSys’s higher numerical dissipation can suppress attached-boundary-layer TS-wave amplitude, so fine-scale transition predictions may be code- and resolution-sensitive.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical simulations of transition and long-term response of a wind turbine airfoil

title: Scalar dissipation anomaly and scalar-gradient scaling in turbulence: A joint velocity-scalar multifractal view
authors: Dhawal Buaria
abstract: We revisit the problem of scalar dissipation anomaly and scaling of scalar gradients in passive scalar turbulence using theory and data from well-resolved direct numerical simulations (DNS) on grid sizes of up to $8192^3$, spanning Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers $Re_λ=140-1000$ and Schmidt numbers $Sc = 1-512$. The theory is based on a joint multifractal description of longitudinal velocity increments and scalar increments, constrained by Yaglom's law and extended to gradients via a fluctuating Batchelor cutoff scale. The DNS data show that the normalized mean scalar dissipation approaches a single asymptotic value as both $Re_λ$ and $Sc$ increase, although larger $Sc$ requires larger $\re$ to reach this state. In the multifractal framework, this corresponds to an effective scalar Hölder exponent tending to zero, associated with sharp cliff-like scalar fronts, and saturation of inertial-range scaling scalar structure-function exponents. The joint velocity-scalar fractal dimension of the dissipative structures is inferred to approach $7/3$, indicating a non-space-filling support. The framework further predicts that for fixed $Re_λ$, higher-order central moments of scalar gradients are independent of $Sc$. This prediction is confirmed by DNS data and by the collapse of standardized probability distributions of scalar-gradient across Schmidt numbers. These results suggest that the $Sc$-scaling of scalar gradients is dictated solely by scalar dissipation anomaly. In contrast, their $Re_λ$-dependence reflects strong intermittency, which can be directly related to mixed velocity-scalar structure function exponents.

infographic.key_insight: Scalar dissipation in passive-scalar turbulence reaches a universal anomalous limit at high Reynolds and Schmidt numbers, with scalar-gradient intermittency governed by a joint velocity-scalar multifractal cascade.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This helps predict mixing and scalar-gradient extremes in high-Schmidt flows relevant to combustion, contaminant transport, and microscale heat/mass transfer.
method: Joint multifractal model for velocity and scalar increments
Constraint by Yaglom’s law plus fluctuating Batchelor cutoff
DNS-based scaling analysis of scalar dissipation and gradient statistics
infographic.evidence_signal: Well-resolved DNS up to 8192^3, Reλ=140–1000, and Sc=1–512 show collapse of normalized dissipation and standardized scalar-gradient PDFs, supporting the predicted asymptotic and Sc-independent gradient moments.
infographic.watch_item: The asymptotic scaling requires very high Reλ at large Sc, so finite-resolution simulations or experiments may under-resolve the Batchelor scale and delay convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Scalar dissipation anomaly and scalar-gradient scaling in turbulence: A joint velocity-scalar multifractal view

title: Wave turbulence theory of odd fluids and solids: kinetic equations and solutions
authors: Xander M. de Wit, Léo Touzo, Sébastien Galtier, Michel Fruchart, Federico Toschi, Vincenzo Vitelli
abstract: The theory of wave turbulence describes the properties of physical systems composed of a set of weak-amplitude random waves interacting nonlinearly. Here, we study odd wave turbulence, which arises in chiral media subjected to non-reciprocal stresses, notably odd viscosity and odd elasticity. In both cases, we consider simple models for which we can derive and solve analytically the kinetic equations describing the long-term statistical behavior of spectral quantities such as energy or wave action. For odd viscosity, we consider a three-dimensional model that exhibits wave turbulence involving three-wave interactions, which gives rise to a direct energy cascade characterized by an anisotropic Kolmogorov-Zakharov (KZ) spectrum. For odd elasticity, we consider a quasi-one-dimensional overdamped model that exhibits much slower dynamics involving six-wave interactions. In that case, the KZ spectrum corresponding to a forward cascade of a conserved quantity we call odd energy, is nonlocal and therefore does not constitute a physical solution. However, the other KZ solution, which describes an inverse cascade of wave action, is only marginally non-local and is therefore valid up to a logarithmic correction. These two analytical theories provide a rigorous interpretation of direct numerical simulations, where the KZ spectrum is observed both in the case of odd viscosity (forward cascade) and of odd elasticity (inverse cascade).

infographic.key_insight: Odd viscosity and odd elasticity support distinct wave-turbulence cascades that can be captured analytically by kinetic equations, yielding anisotropic direct energy transport in 3D and an inverse wave-action cascade in quasi-1D.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results give a predictive framework for designing and diagnosing chiral active materials and metamaterials where non-reciprocal stresses control how fluctuations and energy move across scales.
method: Derive kinetic equations for weakly nonlinear random waves in odd-fluid and odd-solid models.
Solve the resulting Kolmogorov–Zakharov spectra analytically for three-wave and six-wave interaction regimes.
Compare the predicted cascade directions and spectra with direct numerical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the analytical KZ spectra match direct numerical simulations for both odd viscosity (forward cascade) and odd elasticity (inverse cascade).
infographic.watch_item: The forward-cascade KZ solution for odd elasticity is nonlocal and therefore unphysical, while the valid inverse-cascade solution is only marginally nonlocal and requires a logarithmic correction.
infographic.paper_title: Wave turbulence theory of odd fluids and solids: kinetic equations and solutions

title: Effect of Additively Manufactured Wall Lattice Structures on Flashback Limits in a Hydrogen Jet Flame Combustor
authors: Alexander Jaeschke, Thomas Ludwig Kaiser, Lukas Melzig, Michael F. Zaeh, Kilian Oberleithner, Christian Oliver Paschereit
abstract: This study investigated how additively manufactured nozzles with body-centered cubic lattice structures reduce the flame flashback propensity in a hydrogen jet flame burner. Five different configurations of a jet flame combustor were investigated, with a focus on mixing duct walls incorporating porous media. The nozzles were manufactured by the powder bed fusion of metals using a laser beam process. The lattice parameters were varied by the volume fraction and the strut diameter. For the experiments, pure hydrogen was used as fuel under atmospheric conditions at various equivalence ratios and Reynolds numbers of 9,000 - 12,000. Flow field measurements, flame imaging, and spectral proper orthogonal decomposition of the flame dynamics were employed to identify possible transition mechanisms from a stable operation to flashback. The flow fields and the flame shapes showed only minor effects from wall modifications, preserving general flow characteristics across configurations. The flow dynamics in the combustion chamber were dominated by large-scale coherent structures in the shear layer, specifically Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities. The results demonstrated that the nozzle with the coarsest porous wall structure significantly improved the flashback resistance compared to a nozzle with a solid wall. It is concluded that the primary mitigation mechanism was a cooling effect by unburnt mixture flowing through the porous media. The findings confirmed that the integration of lattice structures through additive manufacturing provides a viable strategy for hydrogen flashback mitigation by manipulating the coupled interaction between the flame and the thermal conditions of the wall.

infographic.key_insight: Additively manufactured porous wall lattices can raise hydrogen flashback limits mainly by cooling the incoming mixture near the wall, rather than by strongly changing the overall flow pattern.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Wall-integrated lattice structures offer a practical passive design lever for improving hydrogen combustor safety and flashback resistance without major changes to core combustor aerodynamics.
method: 5 combustor nozzle configurations compared
Body-centered cubic lattice walls varied by volume fraction and strut diameter
Flow-field imaging and SPOD used to track flashback precursors
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Reynolds numbers of 9,000–12,000 and multiple equivalence ratios, the coarsest porous wall configuration showed the strongest flashback resistance, while flow and flame shapes changed only modestly.
infographic.watch_item: The benefit appears geometry- and operating-condition dependent, so pressure drop, manufacturability, durability, and scale-up effects need validation before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Effect of Additively Manufactured Wall Lattice Structures on Flashback Limits in a Hydrogen Jet Flame Combustor

title: Machine learning for rarefied gas transport in vacuum and micro/nano systems: promise, pitfalls, and a verification agenda
authors: Ehsan Roohi
abstract: Machine learning is beginning to influence rarefied-gas modeling at multiple levels, including equation-solving, operator learning, learned collision physics, moment closures, direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) field surrogates, and gas--surface models. This Perspective argues that the central challenge is not demonstration-level success, but trustworthy use under realistic deployment conditions: multiregime Knudsen behavior, stochastic DSMC labels, sharp nonequilibrium structures, uncertain gas--surface interaction, and scarce direct experimental anchors. I classify the main method families by what is learned, distinguish soft physics penalties from structure-preserving designs, and propose evaluation standards based on extrapolation tests, noise-aware metrics, end-to-end cost accounting, and a three-level validation hierarchy. Most current evidence is solver-facing: it demonstrates surrogate fidelity to a teacher solver more often than direct physical fidelity to experiment. The aim is not to dismiss ML for rarefied and vacuum-related gas transport, but to separate what is already credible from what remains provisional, and to define a reporting standard that makes future claims auditable.

infographic.key_insight: Machine learning can accelerate rarefied-gas transport modeling, but its real value depends on trustworthy performance across multiregime Knudsen behavior, noisy DSMC labels, and weak experimental grounding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For vacuum and micro/nano systems, ML surrogates may reduce solver cost and broaden modeling capability, but only if they are validated beyond teacher-solver imitation and under realistic deployment conditions.
method: Classifies ML approaches by what is learned: solvers, operators, collision physics, closures, DSMC surrogates, and gas--surface models.
Distinguishes soft physics penalties from structure-preserving designs.
Recommends extrapolation testing, noise-aware metrics, end-to-end cost accounting, and a three-level validation hierarchy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract indicates that most current evidence is solver-facing, showing surrogate agreement with teacher solvers more often than direct physical agreement with experiments.
infographic.watch_item: A major concern is that apparent accuracy may not generalize under sharp nonequilibrium structures, uncertain gas--surface interactions, or scarce experimental anchors.
infographic.paper_title: Machine learning for rarefied gas transport in vacuum and micro/nano systems: promise, pitfalls, and a verification agenda

title: Topological origin of flow distributions in disordered porous media
authors: Jose Arnal, Guillem Sole-Mari, Tomás Aquino
abstract: We investigate steady Stokes flow through porous media composed of two-dimensional disordered arrays of circular obstacles. We develop a theory for the statistics of flow rates based on a pore-network model that captures local flow correlations. We show that the flow rate distribution across the ensemble of pore bodies follows a Gamma distribution, and that the flow rate distribution through pore throats is fully determined in terms of it. Furthermore, this Gamma distribution can be directly linked to simple geometrical properties such as the coefficient of variation of pore throat widths, rendering the model parameterisable from minimal medium information. The resulting predictions agree closely with computational fluid dynamics simulations and show markedly better agreement than prior mean-field models that neglect local flow-rate correlations, clarifying how local splitting and merging shape flow in disordered porous networks.

infographic.key_insight: Local flow splitting and merging in disordered pore networks produces Gamma-distributed pore-body flow rates, which in turn determine throat flow statistics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a low-parameter way to predict flow heterogeneity in porous media from simple geometry, useful for designing and analyzing filters, catalysts, and subsurface flows.
method: Build a pore-network model for steady Stokes flow in 2D disordered arrays of circular obstacles
Capture local flow correlations from splitting and merging at pore junctions
Link the Gamma distribution parameter to the coefficient of variation of pore-throat widths
infographic.evidence_signal: The theory matches computational fluid dynamics simulations closely and outperforms prior mean-field models that ignore local flow-rate correlations.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is developed for steady Stokes flow in two-dimensional disordered porous media, so extension to inertial, transient, or fully 3D settings may require new validation.
infographic.paper_title: Topological origin of flow distributions in disordered porous media

title: Impact of alignments between fluctuating and mean density gradients on the scale-dependent energetics of stably stratified turbulence
authors: Soumak Bhattacharjee, Stephen M. de Bruyn Kops, Andrew D. Bragg
abstract: Non-trivial alignments between vorticity and the strain-rate tensor play an important role in the evolution of velocity gradients and the energy cascade in isotropic turbulence. Here we explore how alignments between the fluctuating and mean density gradients impact the mechanisms governing the turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) and available potential energy (APE) across scales in stably stratified turbulence. This is motivated by analytical results that demonstrate a connection between them, and is conducted using direct numerical simulations (DNS) of statistically stationary, stably stratified turbulence for $Pr = 1, 7, 50$ in the strongly stratified regime. After demonstrating how the gradient field alignments depend on scale and $Pr$, we show that the alignments are intimately connected to the reversal of the buoyancy flux at small-scales, and that regions of strong alignment and misalignment correspond to regions where the horizontal TKE inter-scale flux becomes weak. The same is also true of the APE flux, except that at larger scales, regions of strong alignment are associated with an upscale APE flux. The TKE and APE dissipation rates, and the mixing coefficient also show a strong dependence on the alignment, especially for $Pr=1$. Finally, we explore the connection between the local alignment and stability of the flow, and we find a non-trivial relationship, with regions of strong alignment surprisingly occurring most often in stable regions. This demonstrates that the dynamical significance of the alignments on the flow energetics cannot be understood through a simple connection between the local alignments and local stability of the flow.

infographic.key_insight: Scale-dependent alignments between fluctuating and mean density gradients strongly regulate energy transfer, buoyancy flux reversal, and dissipation in stably stratified turbulence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For stratified flows, subgrid and mixing models should account for local gradient alignment because it changes TKE/APE fluxes, dissipation, and mixing efficiency across scales.
method: Direct numerical simulations of statistically stationary strongly stratified turbulence
Compared Pr = 1, 7, and 50
Analyzed gradient-field alignments, inter-scale fluxes, buoyancy flux, and dissipation across scales
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports DNS-based analysis showing alignment-dependent changes in buoyancy flux reversal, horizontal TKE and APE fluxes, dissipation rates, and mixing coefficient, with the strongest effects at Pr = 1.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions are drawn from stationary DNS in the strongly stratified regime, so the alignment–energetics relationships may not transfer directly to weaker stratification or practical Reynolds-number flows without validation.
infographic.paper_title: Impact of alignments between fluctuating and mean density gradients on the scale-dependent energetics of stably stratified turbulence

title: Nested homogenization of xylem-inspired porous fluidic networks
authors: Pier Giuseppe Ledda, Giacomo Ferrari, Giuseppe Antonio Zampogna
abstract: Xylem transport relies on a hierarchy of vessels, pits, and porous membranes that redistribute the flow across several length scales. Directly resolving this nested architecture is computationally prohibitive for network-scale studies, while existing reduced models often require prescribed inter-vessel hydraulic resistances. Here, we develop a nested homogenization framework for rigid porous membranes under single-phase viscous flow. The approach first replaces the pore-scale structure of a membrane by an effective stress-jump interface law, and then embeds this effective interface inside a second characteristic problem to obtain a conduit-scale closure for pit-mediated exchange. In this way, pore-scale geometry is systematically propagated to network-scale hydraulic response through effective tensors. The reduced model is compared against fully resolved simulations in simplified xylem-inspired vessel connections, showing that the homogenized description captures the pressure drop and flow redistribution. Finally, the resulting interface law is embedded within a xylem-like network with randomly disabled conducting elements, demonstrating that the model is suitable to describe the emergent hydraulic response from the coupling between local membrane-mediated transfer and network topology. The framework provides a tractable route for studying multiscale porous fluidic networks and forms a basis for extensions involving deformable structures and multiphase flows.

infographic.key_insight: A nested homogenization strategy turns pore-scale xylem membrane geometry into an effective interface law, then into a conduit-scale closure for network-level flow exchange.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a tractable multiscale model for predicting pressure drop and flow redistribution in porous fluidic networks without resolving every pore or prescribing ad hoc resistances.
method: Homogenize the rigid porous membrane to an effective stress-jump interface law at the pore scale.
Embed that interface in a second characteristic problem to derive conduit-scale pit-mediated exchange coefficients.
Propagate microgeometry to network-scale response through effective tensors in a xylem-inspired network model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The reduced model is validated against fully resolved simulations in simplified vessel connections and then tested in a network with randomly disabled conduits, matching pressure drop and flow redistribution trends.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is developed for rigid, single-phase membranes, so deformability, multiphase effects, and complex real-world tissue variability may require further extension.
infographic.paper_title: Nested homogenization of xylem-inspired porous fluidic networks

title: Ultimate regime in Rayleigh-Darcy Convection
authors: Garima Varshney, Anikesh Pal, Narsimha Reddy Rapaka
abstract: DNS of Rayleigh-Darcy convection in a 3D porous domain is performed at Ra $\in [10^3, 10^6]$ to investigate heat-transfer scaling, thermal boundary-layer dynamics, and flow-structure evolution in the unexplored ultimate regime. The Nu exhibits an approximately linear dependence on Ra throughout the investigated range. However, a distinct change in slope is observed at $Ra \approx 4\times10^5$, indicating the onset of the ultimate regime. For $Ra \leq 2.5\times10^5$, our scaling is 6.25% lower than that reported by \cite{hewitt2014high}, while for $Ra \geq 4\times10^5$ our results are within 1.24% of the extrapolated ultimate-regime prediction of \cite{pirozzoli2021towards}. Analysis of thermal structure reveals formation of near-wall protoplumes that merge into large-scale columnar megaplumes. With increasing Ra, the size of the protoplumes decreases, whereas the numbers increase, thus enhancing boundary-layer convection and heat transport. The thermal boundary-layer thickness scales as ~ Ra^{-1} and ~ Nu^{-1}, corroborating the persistence of linear heat-transfer scaling in the ultimate regime. The thermal dissipation is found to be increasingly shifting from the boundary layer to the bulk with increasing $Ra$, further indicating that the finer protoplumes efficiently transport heat from walls to bulk. The flow structures are quantified using the dominant length scale using the mean wavenumber ($\overline{k}$). It exhibits linear variation with $Ra$ for near-wall structures, with a higher slope in the ultimate regime, signifying finer protoplumes. At the mid-plane, a weaker scaling suggests that the megaplumes also become finer with increasing $Ra$ in the ultimate regime, thus leading to efficient heat transport in the bulk.

infographic.key_insight: Rayleigh-Darcy convection in porous media shows an approximately linear Nu–Ra law up to 10^6, with a clear slope change near Ra ≈ 4×10^5 marking the onset of the ultimate regime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests that high-Rayleigh porous systems can sustain increasingly efficient heat transport through finer near-wall and bulk plume structures, which is important for thermal management and geothermal/porous-media design.
method: 3D DNS of Rayleigh-Darcy convection in a porous domain
Sweep over Ra ∈ [10^3, 10^6] to track Nu scaling and flow-structure evolution
Quantify boundary-layer thickness, thermal dissipation partition, and dominant length scale via mean wavenumber
infographic.evidence_signal: The observed Nu scaling is 6.25% below prior results for Ra ≤ 2.5×10^5, while for Ra ≥ 4×10^5 it matches the extrapolated ultimate-regime prediction within 1.24%.
infographic.watch_item: The reported regime transition is inferred from DNS over a finite Ra range, so extrapolation to other porous geometries, permeability models, or higher Ra should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Ultimate regime in Rayleigh-Darcy Convection

title: Bacterial adhesion to curved surfaces in fluid flow
authors: Edwina F. Yeo, Benjamin J. Walker, Philip Pearce, Mohit P. Dalwadi
abstract: Minimising bacterial surface adhesion and subsequent biofilm formation in industrial and medical settings requires understanding how bacteria are transported and adhere to complex surface geometries in the presence of non-uniform flow. In this paper, we consider the transport of a dilute suspension of motile bacteria through a corrugated two-dimensional channel with perfectly adhesive walls. We asymptotically analyse the diffusive boundary layer that forms in high velocity flows using a curvilinear coordinate system based on the fluid streamfunction, presenting a similarity solution to the diffusivity-varying diffusion-type equation that arises. From this solution, we derive an analytical expression for the bacterial adhesion rate as a function of surface arclength and the spatially varying wall shear rate. Our model predicts that bacterial adhesion becomes localised on curved surfaces, with bacteria showing preferential adhesion to wall `peaks' at lower shear rates and preferential adhesion to wall `valleys' at higher shear rates. More broadly, our results highlight how spatially varying flows generated by complex geometries can lead to localised bacterial adhesion, with potential implications for both enhancing and minimising biofilm formation.

infographic.key_insight: Curved channel geometry and spatially varying shear can localise bacterial adhesion, shifting attachment toward wall peaks at lower shear and wall valleys at higher shear.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result helps predict and control biofilm risk in industrial and medical flow systems by linking surface shape and flow conditions to where bacteria are most likely to stick.
method: Asymptotic analysis of the high-velocity diffusive boundary layer
Curvilinear coordinate system based on the fluid streamfunction
Similarity solution for a diffusivity-varying diffusion-type equation
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports an analytical adhesion-rate expression derived from the model and its comparison is based on predicted spatial localisation patterns rather than experimental data.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is analytical and asymptotic, so accuracy may be limited outside the high-velocity, dilute-suspension regime or for more complex wall properties.
infographic.paper_title: Bacterial adhesion to curved surfaces in fluid flow

title: Spectrally Regularized Latent Flow Matching for Turbulence Generation
authors: Khalid Rafiq, Aditya G. Nair
abstract: Latent diffusion and flow matching have emerged as leading approaches for synthetic turbulence generation, yet they systematically under-represent dissipation-range amplitudes. We introduce a latent flow matching framework with a spectrally regularized compression stage that directly targets this failure mode. On a 256^2 DNS dataset at Re_f \approx 2250, replacing an MSE-trained VAE with a zone-weighted log-spectral objective raises deep-dissipation retained spectral power from 25% to 94% in reconstruction and from 20% to 79% in unconditional generation. The improved latent representation also yields a substantially better sampling cost-fidelity tradeoff: the MSE-trained latent space imposes a fundamental quality ceiling near DD bias -0.70 that no integrator or step-count can overcome, while the spectrally regularized latent space reaches DD bias -0.117 at just 20 function evaluations. Mechanistically, encoder-decoder swap experiments show that the improvement is driven primarily by encoder-induced latent reorganization rather than decoder capacity, while a support-amplitude decomposition reveals that MSE-trained models behave as conservative suppression models, minimizing pointwise error by attenuating intermittent high-wavenumber structure. Both pipelines recover the second-order structure function and the correct sign of S_3, indicating the correct cascade direction without explicit supervision. A small residual gap in the magnitude of S_3 suggests that phase-coherent triadic organization remains a complementary axis to amplitude fidelity for future generative turbulence models.

infographic.key_insight: A spectrally regularized latent compression stage dramatically improves latent flow matching for turbulence by preserving dissipation-range amplitudes that MSE-trained VAEs suppress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This yields far better sample fidelity at low inference cost, making generative turbulence models more practical for reduced-order simulation and data-driven flow synthesis.
method: Replace an MSE-trained VAE with a spectrally regularized, zone-weighted log-spectral encoder-decoder.
Train latent flow matching on the improved latent space for unconditional turbulence generation.
Use encoder-decoder swap and support-amplitude analyses to isolate where spectral fidelity gains originate.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a 256^2 DNS dataset at Re_f ≈ 2250, deep-dissipation retained spectral power improved from 25% to 94% in reconstruction and from 20% to 79% in generation, with DD bias improving to -0.117 at 20 function evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract notes a residual magnitude gap in S_3, suggesting phase-coherent triadic structure is still imperfect and may limit full physical realism.
infographic.paper_title: Spectrally Regularized Latent Flow Matching for Turbulence Generation

title: A fully GPU-based workflow for building physics emulators of hypersonic flows
authors: Fabian Paischer, Dylan Rubini, Deniz A. Bezgin, Aaron B. Buhendwa, David Hauser, Florian Sestak
abstract: The ability to resolve complex physical phenomena with high fidelity and at low computational cost is central to addressing key challenges in modern engineering. A prime example lies in hypersonic flows, where the precise prediction of the full flowfield topology, in particular with respect to shock wave location and intensity, is critical. Yet supersonic and hypersonic flows continue to be a stumbling block for traditional reduced-order models and neural emulators that struggle to capture steep gradients in flow states with physical consistency in applications of industrial relevance. To that end, we introduce a fully GPU based workflow that integrates accelerated data generation with the training of neural emulators augmented by uncertainty quantification and physics-aware refinement. Our workflow is enabled by a differentiable high-fidelity solver (JAX-Fluids) which we employ for rapid dataset creation and residual-based improvement of the neural emulator to enhance physical consistency. Building on this framework, we first present a suite of model architectures and analyze their scaling behavior to expose their strengths and shortcomings. We then show that residual-based refinement enables training on cases where only mesh and input parameters are available, substantially reducing residuals and improving physical consistency. Together, differentiable simulation and residual-based refinement yield physics emulators that remain reliable beyond their training distribution, a key requirement for deploying surrogates in real-world engineering design loops.

infographic.key_insight: A fully GPU-based pipeline combines differentiable high-fidelity simulation, neural emulation, and residual-based refinement to produce physics-consistent hypersonic flow surrogates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, lower-cost prediction of shock-dominated flowfields for design and optimization workflows where accurate hypersonic aerodynamics are critical.
method: Use JAX-Fluids to generate training data on GPU with a differentiable high-fidelity solver.
Train neural emulators with uncertainty quantification and compare multiple architectures for scaling behavior.
Apply residual-based refinement to improve physical consistency, especially when only mesh and input parameters are available.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that residual-based refinement substantially reduces residuals, improves physical consistency, and extends reliability beyond the training distribution.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may still depend on architecture choice and the quality/coverage of the training distribution, especially for steep shock gradients and extrapolation cases.
infographic.paper_title: A fully GPU-based workflow for building physics emulators of hypersonic flows

title: Explicit Quantum Circuit Simulation of Nonlinear 1-Dimensional Fluid with Carleman-linearized Boltzmann Method
authors: Keita Kanno, Kazumasa Ueno, Hayato Higuchi, Morimasa Okamoto, Yuya Yoshizuru, Ryoya Ishimaru
abstract: Quantum computation of fluid dynamics has attracted growing attention as a key application of fault-tolerant quantum computers anticipated in the coming decade, with lattice Boltzmann methods emerging as a particularly promising approach. Explicit and efficient elementary-gate-level circuit simulations, however, have so far been demonstrated only in the linear case. Here we include the leading nonlinearity through second-order Carleman linearization of the one-dimensional Boltzmann equation, and demonstrate, via explicit quantum-circuit simulation, the preparation of the final-time state using a Taylor-expansion-based ODE solver based on the quantum singular value transformation. With this construction, we analyze the gate and qubit complexities, which scale logarithmically with the grid size, the nonlinearity captured by the higher-order Carleman linearization, and the practical utility of higher-order expansions in the Taylor ODE solver. The construction provides a concrete baseline for computational cost reduction and further developments such as extensions to higher dimensions, complex geometries, and the extraction of physical quantities, towards industrially useful quantum CFD.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that a 1D nonlinear Boltzmann fluid model can be simulated on a fault-tolerant quantum computer by combining second-order Carleman linearization with a QSVT-based Taylor ODE solver.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a concrete quantum-CFD cost baseline, with gate and qubit complexity that grows only logarithmically with grid size, suggesting a path toward scalable fluid simulation on future quantum hardware.
method: Model the 1D Boltzmann equation with second-order Carleman linearization to capture leading nonlinearity.
Use a Taylor-expansion ODE solver based on quantum singular value transformation to prepare the final-time state.
Analyze circuit cost at the elementary-gate level for the explicit quantum simulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports explicit quantum-circuit simulations and complexity analysis for final-time state preparation, rather than experimental fluid data.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is still demonstrated only for a 1D model and depends on fault-tolerant quantum hardware, so practical utility for real CFD remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Explicit Quantum Circuit Simulation of Nonlinear 1-Dimensional Fluid with Carleman-linearized Boltzmann Method

title: Two pathways to diapycnal mixing in strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear
authors: Pascale Garaud, Dante Buhl, Jason Johnstone, Arstanbek Tulekeyev, Nathan van Duker
abstract: While vertically-sheared stratified flows have been studied extensively, their horizontally-sheared counterparts have received considerably less attention. Yet, horizontal shear instabilities remain active even when the mean Richardson number is large or even formally infinite, and can drive turbulence in strongly stratified (low Froude number) flows at sufficiently high Reynolds number. In this work, we combine linear theory with direct numerical simulations to investigate two pathways to turbulence in low Froude / high Reynolds number horizontally-sheared flow with no initial vertical shear. In the first pathway, vertical shear emerges directly from vertically-modulated eigenmodes of the primary horizontal shear instability, and becomes unstable to secondary small-scale Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH) instabilities on the buoyancy scale at sufficiently large buoyancy Reynolds number $Re_b$. In the second pathway, a vertically-invariant eigenmode of the primary horizontal shear instability initially dominates, causing the background flow to evolve nonlinearly into a long-lived time-dependent two-dimensional (columnar) vortical flow. The vortices are subsequently unstable to secondary three-dimensional hyperbolic instabilities from which vertical shear emerges, which is finally unstable to tertiary small-scale KH instabilities on the buoyancy scale at sufficiently large $Re_b$. This shows that the emergence of vertical shear driving small-scale KH instabilities is an inevitable by-product of horizontal shear instabilities in strongly stratified flows at sufficiently large $Re_b$. However, we also find that the two pathways excite different ranges of vertical scales, which results in different peak mixing efficiencies.

infographic.key_insight: In strongly stratified, horizontally sheared flows with no initial vertical shear, turbulence can arise through two distinct routes, but both ultimately generate vertical shear that triggers small-scale Kelvin–Helmholtz mixing at sufficiently high buoyancy Reynolds number.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This identifies when nominally horizontal shear in stratified geophysical or industrial flows can still drive diapycnal mixing, helping predict mixing efficiency and vertical transport in high-Re, low-Froude regimes.
method: Linear stability analysis of horizontally sheared stratified flow
Direct numerical simulations to follow nonlinear evolution and secondary instabilities
Comparison of two pathways: vertically modulated primary modes versus columnar vortical evolution
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports combined linear theory and DNS showing two instability pathways and their different excited vertical-scale ranges, which produce different peak mixing efficiencies.
infographic.watch_item: The results depend on sufficiently large buoyancy Reynolds number, so the mixing pathways and efficiencies may not apply at lower-Re or less strongly stratified conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Two pathways to diapycnal mixing in strongly stratified flows with no initial vertical shear
